heading.en: Why is the sand hot but the sea cool?

hook.en: On a sunny day at Malpe beach the sand burns your feet while the sea stays cool. Both get the same sunshine, but water needs far more heat to warm up.

title.en: Define heat capacity and specific heat capacity

say.en: On a sunny day at Malpe beach the sand burns your feet while the sea stays cool. Both get the same sunshine, but water needs far more heat to warm up. In this lesson: Define heat capacity and specific heat capacity.
Apply the principle of calorimetry.

body.en: The heat needed to raise the temperature of a body is Q = msΔT. The *specific heat capacity* s is the heat needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1 K, in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Heat capacity S = ΔQ/ΔT is for the whole body. Molar specific heat capacity is per mole. Water has a very high s, about 4186 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, which is why it is used in car radiators and why coastal climates are mild.
body.kn: Q = msΔT. 1 kg ವಸ್ತುವಿನ ತಾಪವನ್ನು 1 K ಹೆಚ್ಚಿಸಲು ಬೇಕಾದ ಉಷ್ಣವೇ ವಿಶಿಷ್ಟೋಷ್ಣ ಸಾಮರ್ಥ್ಯ s. ನೀರಿನ s ಸುಮಾರು 4186 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, ಬಹಳ ಹೆಚ್ಚು. ಆದ್ದರಿಂದ ಕರಾವಳಿ ಹವಾಮಾನ ಸೌಮ್ಯ.

say.en: The heat needed to raise the temperature of a body is Q equals msdelta T. The specific heat capacity s is the heat needed to raise 1 kilogram of a substance by 1 kelvin, in J kg to the power minus 1 K to the power minus 1. Heat capacity S equals delta Q over delta T is for the whole body. Molar specific heat capacity is per mole. Water has a very high s, about 4186 joules kg to the power minus 1 K to the power minus 1, which is why it is used in car radiators and why coastal climates are mild. Q equals m s delta T.

Heat to raise a mass m by ΔT is m s ΔT, where s is the specific heat capacity. Water has a large s, 4186 joule per kilogram kelvin.
Drop a hot body into cold water. Heat lost by the hot body equals heat gained by the water.
One hundred grams of copper at 100 degrees into two hundred grams of water at 20 degrees. The mixture settles near 23.6 degrees, close to the water's start.

narration.en: Let us solve this together. A 0.1 kg metal block at 100 °C is dropped into 0.2 kg of water at 20 °C. The final temperature is 25 °C. Find the specific heat of the metal, ignoring the calorimeter. (s_water = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)

say.en: Let us solve this together. A 0.1 kilograms metal block at 100 degrees Celsius is dropped into 0.2 kilograms of water at 20 degrees Celsius. The final temperature is 25 degrees Celsius. Find the specific heat of the metal, ignoring the calorimeter. (s water equals 4200 joules kg to the power minus 1 K to the power minus 1).
Heat gained by water equals 0.2 times 4200 times 25 minus 20 equals 4200 joules.
Heat lost by metal equals 0.1 times s times 100 minus 25 equals 7.5 seconds.
7.5 seconds equals 4200 gives s equals 560 joules kg to the power minus 1 K to the power minus 1.
So the answer is 560 joules kg to the power minus 1 K to the power minus 1.
